lessons.title: Formulation as clinical method: what it is, what it is not, and how it differs from a diagnosis
lessons.explanation: Earlier lessons introduced the idea of a formulation as a testable map of a person's difficulties. This lesson goes inside the method. A formulation is an analytical and evaluative account of why this particular person, in this particular situation, is having these particular difficulties now. A diagnosis, by contrast, is a classification: it names a recognised pattern so that clinicians can communicate, compare populations, and connect a presentation to a body of research. Gareth Owen's 2023 review puts the contrast in one sentence: when two experts assess the same patient they may produce two similar summaries but two different formulations, because a summary is descriptive while a formulation is analytical and evaluative [1]. That is not a defect to be engineered away. Two clinicians can share every fact and still weigh them differently, because a formulation contains argument, not only observation. The idea has a history worth knowing because the current version is a compromise between two extremes. Adolf Meyer, at Johns Hopkins from 1910, argued that a person arrives with a complaint rather than a disease entity, and that the complaint should be understood through the whole life course of their organ systems, instincts and life events; he taught the life chart as a tool and preferred what he called a formulation of the available facts of each case to assigning a standard entity, treating each case as an experiment of nature [1]. George Engel extended a similar pluralism to the whole of medicine in 1977, arguing that the biopsychosocial approach was the true medical model rather than a psychiatric special case [1]. Both contributions are broad and both are short on operational detail, and Owen records the consequences: the influential postwar textbook Clinical Psychiatry called Meyer's approach almost entirely sterile, and a later leading British textbook said the concept of formulation is too muddled for the examination room [1]. The practical answer to that muddle was the four Ps, a grid that applies predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protecting factors across biological, psychological and social domains. Its discipline is the point: each proposed cause needs an evidence base for its causal role and each proposed intervention needs evidence that it modifies that cause [1]. Everything below is education about clinical reasoning using fictional material. It is not a method for diagnosing anyone, and it does not tell anyone what treatment to seek.
lessons.example: Take a fictional 40-year-old man who has arrived in a new country as an asylum seeker and who presents to a general practitioner with six months of low mood, poor sleep, weight loss, poor concentration and daily drinking. Owen uses a version of this case to show the 4P grid in operation [1]. The biological row lists sleep deprivation and alcohol under perpetuating causes, with the treatments pointed at those causes being sleep advice and alcohol education. The psychological row lists stress and anxiety, with psychoeducation and anxiety management as the interventions. The social row lists migration, uncertain immigration status and social and cultural isolation, and here the treatment column names social and legal advocacy and support groups. Read the grid carefully and something important becomes visible: the social row is the one carrying the most weight, and it is also the row where a clinician cannot act alone. A formulation that named only the alcohol and the insomnia would be coherent, evidence-based in its parts, and completely wrong about the case. Now apply the same grid to a person with the same diagnosis but a different life. A fictional 40-year-old woman with a first episode of severe depression after a bereavement, with no migration history, a stable job, and a family history of depression, produces a different grid in every cell, and therefore a different plan, even though the diagnostic label may be identical. Owen's own summary of the model's value is worth keeping: he notes that some causal factors are not modifiable, and that highlighting areas of powerlessness may itself be one of the strengths of the model [1]. Stated plainly, a good formulation sometimes documents that nothing can currently be changed, which is more honest and more useful than a plan that pretends otherwise.
lessons.question: Two clinicians have identical notes about a patient but produce different formulations. Does that show that one of them has made an error?
lessons.answer: No. The notes are a summary of observations; a formulation is an evaluative argument built from them, so two defensible arguments can differ while sharing the same facts.
lessons.distractor: Yes. A formulation is a summary written in the first person, so any difference between two accounts of the same facts is a documentation error.
lessons.correction: The distinction between a descriptive summary and an analytical formulation is the heart of the lesson. Differences between formulations are expected and are useful only if each can be stated in a way that others can examine, which is why the next lessons insist on formulations that name their own uncertainties.

depth.definitions: A diagnosis is a named pattern of features that supports communication, research and, for some conditions, treatment selection. A formulation is a collaborative, analysable account of a person's difficulties that explains how predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors interact, and that guides the order in which problems are tackled. A summary is a description of what was found. The biopsychosocial model is Engel's claim that biological, psychological and social levels all belong inside ordinary medical reasoning. Predisposing factors raise the likelihood of difficulty over time, such as a family history or early adversity. Precipitating factors are events close to onset. Perpetuating factors maintain the difficulty now, and they matter most because they are the usual targets of change. Protective factors are strengths, supports and circumstances that reduce risk, and the clinical task is to support rather than remove them. Evidence-based causation means that a factor is included in a formulation only when there is evidence that it can contribute causally, not because the factor is merely plausible or emotionally satisfying [1].
depth.mechanism: Why not simply use diagnoses? Because the evidence for a strong link between any one classification and any one treatment pathway in psychiatry is often weaker than the phrase "evidence-based medicine" invites people to assume. Macneil and colleagues set out the case in detail: they note that diagnosis may tell us little about causation, may instruct poorly about which intervention to choose, and offers no information about the person's experience of their difficulty [2]. They cite Kendell and Jablensky's acknowledgement that many diagnoses are helpful working concepts but are not valid in the sense of being discrete entities with natural boundaries, and they cite the observation that two people can receive the same diagnosis drawn from a checklist while sharing few or even none of the same features [2]. The practical mechanism by which formulation adds value is therefore selection and sequencing. A formulation takes a large set of true observations and produces a small ordered list: what is load-bearing, what is modifiable, what should be attempted first, and what is likely to go wrong during treatment. The second mechanism is accountability. A diagnosis can be right or wrong but it cannot easily be argued with; a formulation states its reasoning, so another professional can point at the step where the reasoning fails. The mechanism has a limit that the same literature names openly: causal inference in an individual case is not the same as a causal effect estimated in a population, and several of the most important factors in a formulation will have only weak individual-level evidence behind them [1].
depth.secondExample: Consider a fictional 22-year-old student who has stopped attending seminars, sleeps through the day, has withdrawn from friends and has unexplained weight loss. Run the same method in two different orders and the point becomes concrete. If the clinician starts from a diagnosis and works forwards, the presentation may be read as depression, and the formulation is then written to fit the label, which quietly suppresses the observations that do not fit: the night-time agitation, the daytime sleeping pattern, the fact that the withdrawal began in one week rather than over months. If the clinician starts from a timeline, the formulation is written first and the label is chosen last, so the week of onset becomes a question, the daytime sleeping becomes a perpetuating factor in its own right, and a physical cause remains formally on the list. The two routes can reach the same conclusion, and the second route leaves a trail that shows how it got there. A further difference appears when a treatment fails. Under the first route, a failed treatment is evidence that the person is resistant or that the case is complex. Under the second, a failed treatment is information about the formulation, since the formulation made a prediction and the prediction did not hold. That is what makes the method testable in ordinary practice, and it is also what the next lesson on levels of care depends on: escalating care is an intervention too, and it should be justified by something in the formulation rather than by how unwell the person looks.
depth.mistake: The most common error is to treat a formulation as a warmer, more humane version of a diagnosis, something a kind clinician writes instead of a label. That reading loses the whole method, because it makes the formulation unfalsifiable. If everything observed can be fitted into the account, the account explains nothing and cannot guide action. A second error is the opposite: to treat formulation as unscientific storytelling and to rely on criteria alone. Criteria answer the question of what this looks like; they do not answer why it is happening to this person now, and the literature reviewed above states explicitly that diagnosis may tell us little about causation [2]. A third, sharper error is the single-cause error, in which one factor is elevated to the cause of everything: childhood adversity explains the mood, the sleep, the drinking and the relationship breakdown. The 4P grid exists to prevent exactly that collapse, because it forces the clinician to place each factor in a domain and a temporal role, and, crucially, to state whether the evidence supports a causal role at all [1]. A fourth error is to write the formulation as a verdict. A formulation is an argument that must be revisable, and a formulation that could not be shown to be wrong is not a formulation but a conviction.
depth.application: Non-blocking task: choose one of the two fictional cases above, or construct your own entirely fictional case, and write a four-by-three grid with the four Ps as rows and biological, psychological and social as columns. Fill every cell with a short phrase. Then annotate the grid: mark each entry E for evidence-based causal claim, P for plausible but unevidenced, or U for unknown. Mark each entry M for modifiable or N for not currently modifiable. Finally write one sentence of the form: "This formulation would be wrong if X were the case." Model response and self-review rubric: a strong grid has at least two domains represented in the perpetuating row, at least one cell marked U or N, and no cell containing a diagnosis as if a diagnosis were a cause. A strong falsifying sentence names a specific observation that could be checked, such as a change in the pattern of drinking, rather than a vague statement such as "if the person did not improve". If your grid has every cell marked E and M, review it: the source literature states plainly that many causative effects are unknown and that some factors are not modifiable, and a grid without U or N entries is usually a grid in which the writer has confused plausibility with evidence [1]. If your grid contains no social row entries, ask whether the assessment has actually asked about housing, income, work, migration status, discrimination and relationships, or whether these were never mentioned and therefore never considered.
depth.summary: A formulation is the analytic layer of clinical reasoning: it explains why this person, here and now, has these difficulties, and it orders the things that could be changed. A diagnosis remains necessary for communication, for some treatment evidence and for research, but it does not by itself answer the causal question, and two people with the same diagnosis can share few or no features. The 4P grid across biological, psychological and social domains gives the method its discipline, requiring each included cause to be evidence-based rather than merely plausible, and it survives the criticism that the biopsychosocial idea is vague by forcing specificity into each cell. What the method cannot do is guarantee correct prediction, and it should not try; its value is that its errors are legible, so they can be corrected in the next conversation rather than discovered at the end of a treatment.

visual.title: From a descriptive summary to a testable formulation, and back again
visual.description: A five-step sequence showing how the same observations become a summary, then an analytical formulation built on a three-domain, four-P grid, then an explicit prediction, then a revision after the prediction is tested in ordinary care. The diagram emphasises that the summary is shared between clinicians while the formulation is argued, and that the arrows run in both directions because a failed prediction is treated as information about the formulation rather than as a fact about the person.
steps: Step 1, observations: the timeline, the person's account, the mental state examination, the physical review and the social circumstances, all recorded without interpretation.

Step 2, descriptive summary: the same facts, ordered and stated plainly; two clinicians with the same notes should produce similar summaries here, and this layer is what other professionals and the person themselves can check.

Step 3, analytical formulation: a grid with three columns, biological, psychological and social, and four rows, predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protecting; every entry marked as evidence-based, plausible or unknown, and as modifiable or not currently modifiable.

Step 4, prediction: one sentence naming the factor the plan is betting on, one sentence naming the observation that would show the formulation is wrong, and one sentence naming who will check it and when.

Step 5, revision: the same grid rewritten after the review, with the changed cells marked; the loop returns to step 3 rather than to step 1, because the observations usually stand while the argument about them changes.

lessons.title: Levels of care and escalation: what crisis, community and inpatient care can actually do
lessons.explanation: "Levels of care" sounds like a ladder from mild to severe, and that metaphor causes most of the confusion in this area. The levels are not grades of illness; they are different service arrangements with different capabilities, different legal powers, different costs and different things they remove from a person's life. The World Health Organization's guidance on community mental health services sets out the shift it wants countries to make away from institutional, biomedical models of care toward person-centred, recovery-oriented and human rights-based approaches aligned with the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, and lists the service types that make up a whole system: mental health crisis services, hospital-based mental health services, community mental health centres, peer support services, community outreach services, supported living, and comprehensive mental health service networks [2]. That list is what "levels" actually means: a portfolio of settings, each with a job. The capability question is the one to ask first. What can this setting do that the current setting cannot? Inpatient care can provide continuous observation, physical health care under one roof, separation from an environment that is being maintained as unsafe, and a legal framework within which a person can be treated without their consent where the law permits. A crisis service working in someone's home can see how the person actually lives, work with the people around them, and avoid the disruption of an admission. A community mental health centre can offer continuity over years. Peer support offers something no profession supplies by imitation, which is the experience of having been through it. Supported living addresses housing, which is a health intervention when the absence of housing is part of what maintains the crisis. The second question is legal: what authority is needed for the proposed action, and what does that authority remove? That question is answered in the next lesson. The third is what the plan will be. NICE's guideline on transition between inpatient mental health settings and community or care home settings begins from principles: the aim of care and support in transition should be person-centred and focused on recovery, people should be worked with as active partners in their own care and transition planning, and people should be supported in the least restrictive setting available [1]. Everything below is education about how services are organised, using fictional examples. It is not advice about any real person's care.
lessons.example: Take a fictional 34-year-old woman with a long history of severe depression who has become unable to eat or sleep, has been drinking more, and whose landlord has begun eviction proceedings. Two colleagues disagree about the level of care. One argues for admission, on the grounds that she is not safe at home. The other argues for an intensive community package. Run the capability test and the disagreement becomes tractable. If the absence of overnight observation is the only thing the home setting cannot provide, then admission answers that and nothing else, and the eviction will still be waiting at discharge. If instead the need is for help with the drinking in an environment where alcohol is constantly available and for advocacy with the housing situation, then a home-based crisis service plus a housing worker may answer more of the actual problem, and admission may postpone rather than address it. The guideline is quite specific about what has to be in place whichever route is taken. Before discharge, a designated person is responsible for writing the care plan in collaboration with the person and, if the person agrees, their carers; the plan is written in clear language without jargon; it is based on recovery principles and describes support arrangements after discharge; and it must include possible relapse signs, recovery goals, who to contact, where to go in a crisis, social networks, education and work activities, details of the treatment and support plan, physical health needs, and the date of review [1]. Notice how many of those items are not clinical at all. A plan without the crisis contact and the review date is not a thin plan; it is a plan that has omitted the two items most likely to determine what happens next. The same guideline adds that discharge planning should cover aftercare support in line with section 117 of the Mental Health Act 1983 and should assess the person's personal, social, safety and practical needs, including where they will live, food, transport, budgeting and benefits, and pre-existing family and social stressors that may have triggered the admission [1]. It also notes that carers' circumstances may have changed since admission, so the plan has to be renegotiated with them rather than assumed [1]. That last point is easy to read past and it is the practical form of the whole lesson: the setting is not the plan, and the plan is not a document.
lessons.question: A person's risk appears unchanged but their housing is about to be lost. Is the correct response to move them to a higher level of care?
lessons.answer: Not necessarily. Escalation is justified by an unmet need that the new setting can actually meet, and the need here may be a housing intervention rather than continuous observation.
lessons.distractor: Yes. Risk that remains unchanged after review always requires the next level of care, since the purpose of escalation is to match risk to observation.
lessons.correction: Escalation is an intervention with its own costs and its own legal consequences, so the test is capability, not severity of appearance. Where the unmet need is accommodation, the guideline's own discharge planning content points at housing action and structured support to find and keep accommodation rather than at admission.

depth.definitions: A level of care is a service arrangement defined by what it can provide, what legal powers it holds and what it costs. Crisis resolution or home treatment teams deliver intensive assessment and support in a person's own setting, usually as an alternative to admission. Inpatient care is hospital-based, with continuous staffing and, where the law allows, the capacity to treat without consent. Community mental health centres provide long-term outpatient care and coordination. Supported living provides accommodation with flexible support. Peer support is delivered by people with lived experience who are formally recruited, trained and supervised. A care plan is the written, shared account of support arrangements, named responsibilities, crisis contacts and review dates. Least restrictive means the option that achieves the purpose while removing the fewest rights and the least freedom of action [1]. Section 117 aftercare refers to a statutory duty in England and Wales following certain detentions. Transition is the movement between settings, including admission as well as discharge, and it is the point of highest planning complexity.
depth.mechanism: Three mechanisms explain why escalation decisions go wrong, and each has a checkable remedy. The first is capability drift. Settings are described in language that carries status, so "inpatient" sounds like more care rather than different care, and the specific capabilities are never listed. The remedy is to make the list explicit before the decision: continuous observation, physical health support, separation from a maintained risk, legal authority, occupational and psychological input, housing assessment. The second is that every setting has a withdrawal as well as an addition. Admission often means leaving work or study, losing contact networks, losing income, and acquiring a record that affects insurance, employment and visas in some jurisdictions; the guideline's insistence on assessing education, work, benefits and budgeting before discharge is the recognition that what was lost during an admission has to be rebuilt [1]. The third is that transitions are themselves risky, which is why a whole NICE guideline exists on the transition between inpatient and community settings and why so much of its content concerns communication, naming a responsible person, and ensuring a date and a contact are written down [1]. The same logic appears in NICE's depression guideline, where referral to specialist mental health services for coordinated multidisciplinary care is framed around specific conditions rather than around how severe the presentation looks: significant impairment of personal and social functioning, no benefit from previous treatments, and either multiple complicating problems such as unemployment or poor housing, or significant coexisting mental and physical health conditions [3]. The multidisciplinary care plan that follows has to name roles and responsibilities, include information about 24-hour support services and how to contact them, and include a crisis plan identifying triggers and strategies [3]. Read those two documents together and the shape of a defensible escalation decision becomes visible: a named unmet need, a named capability, a named legal basis, a named person, and a date.
depth.secondExample: Consider two fictional people whose presentations look similar on a ward round and whose correct answers are opposite. The first is a 19-year-old student who has not slept for four nights, is talking rapidly, has stopped attending everything and is spending money in a way that alarms their family, but who lives with supportive parents, has no history of self-harm and is happy to accept daily visits. The second is a 19-year-old student with the same sleep loss and the same speech pattern, who lives alone in a flat where they have barricaded the door and stopped eating, and who declines all contact. The capability test separates them. In the first case the family home already provides the observation, the food and the continuity that admission would add, so the missing capabilities may be specialist assessment and medication review, which a home treatment team can deliver. In the second case the missing capabilities include continuous observation and physical health monitoring, and access cannot be established voluntarily, which brings the legal question forward. Notice how little work the word "severity" does here. Both people are severely unwell by any reasonable reading, and the differences that decide the question are about environment, consent and access. This is the operational meaning of a levels-of-care decision, and it is also why a service organised as a ladder, where each rung corresponds to how unwell someone seems, produces both unnecessary admissions and unsafe discharges.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first is treating a higher level of care as better care: it is different care, with more restriction and more disruption, and the guideline's own principle is to use the least restrictive setting available [1]. The second is treating community care as automatically less coercive. Community settings can involve compulsion, supervision requirements and pressure, and freedom of movement is not the same as freedom of decision. The third is treating a discharge plan as paperwork. The guideline's content list exists because omissions of the crisis contact or the review date are the failures that show up later, and the plan has to be written with the person, in clear language, and copied to everyone involved in providing support [1]. The fourth is reasoning from availability to justification: if the decision is described as "there is a bed, so we should use it", the reasoning has been replaced by logistics. A related and more subtle error is to confuse the level of care with the level of need, and to conclude that a person who does not need a bed does not need anything, when the unmet need may be housing, money, advocacy or continuity, none of which a hospital provides.
depth.application: Non-blocking task: write the three-column table for one of the fictional cases above. Column one, unmet needs, one line each. Column two, capabilities that would meet each need and which setting holds them, using the WHO service types as the menu: crisis services, hospital-based services, community mental health centres, peer support, outreach, supported living, and the network that connects them [2]. Column three, for each proposed action, whether it can proceed with the person's agreement or whether a legal power is required, and what the person would lose if the action went ahead. Then add the four plan items that a discharge or transition plan cannot omit: possible relapse signs, who to contact, where to go in a crisis, and the date of review [1]. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong table has at least one need that no clinical setting can meet, at least one action that could proceed informally, and a column-three entry that names something the person would lose. A weak table describes all three levels as more or less of the same thing. If your table recommends admission without naming a capability that only admission provides, or recommends community care without naming what would happen if the person's situation deteriorated overnight, revise it before moving on.
depth.summary: The levels of care are a portfolio of settings rather than a severity ladder, and the decision between them turns on three questions asked in order: what unmet need is there, which setting can actually meet it, and what authority is required and what rights does that remove. NICE's transition guideline supplies the operational core of a good decision, which is the least restrictive setting that works, a named person responsible for a shared plan, and specific content in that plan including relapse signs, crisis contact and a review date, plus assessment of the practical circumstances that maintain risk, especially housing and money [1]. NICE's depression guideline shows the same logic in referral criteria and in what a multidisciplinary plan must contain [3]. The limit of the whole apparatus is that it organises care; it does not guarantee that the care is right, and the transition points it emphasises are points of risk precisely because the plan and the reality diverge once the person leaves the building.

visual.title: Three questions between a concern and a change of setting
visual.description: A decision sequence showing that escalation is not a rung on a severity ladder but the output of three ordered questions about unmet need, setting capability and legal authority, followed by a plan with fixed content and a named accountable person. The diagram marks the transition points at both admission and discharge as the places where the plan and reality are most likely to diverge.
steps: Step 1, unmet need: state what is missing or unmanageable now, in functional terms such as access to food, overnight observation, protection from a specific situation at home, or advocacy with housing.

Step 2, capability: name the setting that can meet that need, using the portfolio rather than a ladder: crisis service at home, community mental health centre, supported living, community outreach, peer support, hospital-based care, and the network that links them.
Step 3, authority and cost: decide whether the action can proceed with the person's agreement or requires a legal power, and write down what the person loses if it proceeds at all.

Step 4, plan content: relapse signs, recovery goals, who to contact, where to go in a crisis, medication and treatment details, physical health needs including health promotion, practical circumstances such as accommodation, income and transport, and the review date.

Step 5, named accountability: one designated person writes the plan with the person, copies go to everyone providing support, and carers are told about the plan and the likely discharge date if the person agrees.

Step 6, transition check: at both admission and discharge, re-run steps 1 to 3, because the unmet need and the available capability change and the original decision does not automatically remain correct.

lessons.title: Capacity, consent and coercion: three different ethical problems that are usually confused
lessons.explanation: Three questions get compressed into one in ordinary conversation, and the compression produces bad decisions. The first question is capacity: can this person make this particular decision now? The second is consent: is the agreement or refusal that governs what happens valid, meaning that it is voluntary, informed, and made by someone with capacity for that decision [3]? The third is coercion: what means are being used to influence the person, and are those means justified? These come apart in every direction. A person can have full capacity and still be subjected to pressure; a person can lack capacity and be treated with complete respect; a decision can be lawful and still be ethically questionable. Mental capacity law in England and Wales is built on five principles set out in section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, and it is worth reading them as written. A person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it. A person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them do so have been taken without success. A person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. An act done or decision made for or on behalf of a person who lacks capacity must be done in their best interests. And before the act is done or the decision made, regard must be had to whether the purpose can be achieved in a way that is less restrictive of the person's rights and freedom of action [1]. Section 3 then defines the functional test: a person is unable to make a decision if they cannot understand the information relevant to it, retain that information, use or weigh it as part of the decision process, or communicate their decision by any means. Two provisions guard against over-reading that test: a person is not to be regarded as unable to understand the information if they can understand an explanation given in a way appropriate to their circumstances, using simple language, visual aids or any other means; and the fact that a person can retain the information only for a short period does not by itself prevent them from being regarded as able to make the decision [2]. Note what the test is not. It is not a test of whether the decision is sensible, and it is not a global judgement about a person's mind. This lesson is education about legal and ethical structures using fictional situations. It is not a method for assessing a real person, and it does not recommend or describe any treatment.
lessons.example: Consider three fictional situations in the same hospital. First, a 58-year-old man with a long history of depression has developed a serious physical condition for which clinicians recommend a procedure with a meaningful chance of death without it. He understands the information, can restate it, weighs it in line with his values, and communicates a clear refusal. He has capacity for this decision, and the NHS guidance is explicit about the consequence: if an adult has the capacity to make a voluntary and informed decision to consent to or refuse a particular treatment, that decision must be respected, and this remains the case even if refusing treatment would result in their death or the death of their unborn child [3]. His depression does not change the answer by itself, because a diagnosis is not a finding of incapacity and an unwise decision is not a finding of incapacity [1]. Second, an 79-year-old woman with a urinary infection has become acutely confused overnight, is disoriented to time and place, and is pulling at a drip. She cannot understand or retain the information about a specific intervention at this moment. For that decision, and at that time, she lacks capacity; the appropriate response is to identify and treat the underlying condition, take the decision in her best interests if it cannot wait, involve the people close to her, and revisit the assessment when her confusion has resolved. The delirium guideline discussed in the next lesson makes the same point in clinical terms, directing that where it is difficult to distinguish delirium, dementia, or delirium superimposed on dementia, the delirium should be managed first. Third, a 30-year-old man detained in hospital under section 2 of the Mental Health Act 1983 is being asked to agree to a change in his care arrangements. He is detained, so his liberty is already restricted by law, but that tells us nothing about whether he has capacity to decide this particular question, and the correct approach is to run the capacity test on the actual decision rather than reasoning from the fact of detention. That third case is the one that ordinary reasoning gets wrong most often.
lessons.question: A patient refuses a treatment that the team believes will save his life. Does that refusal by itself establish that he lacks capacity?
lessons.answer: No. The functional test asks whether he can understand, retain, use or weigh the information and communicate a decision, and an unwise decision is expressly not evidence of incapacity.
lessons.distractor: Yes. Where refusal risks death, the decision cannot be voluntary and informed, so the legal test for capacity is not met and treatment may proceed in his best interests.
lessons.correction: Section 1(3) and 1(4) of the Mental Capacity Act separate the quality of the decision from the process of making it, and the NHS guidance states that a capable refusal must be respected even where death may follow. Best-interests decision-making applies when capacity is absent, not when the decision is unwelcome.

depth.definitions: Capacity is a functional, decision-specific and time-specific ability to make a particular decision, defined in section 3 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 by four abilities: understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate [2]. The material time provision means the question is whether the person can decide at the time the decision has to be made, which is why capacity can fluctuate, for example across a delirium. Consent is valid only when it is voluntary, informed and given by a person with capacity for that decision; a signature on a form is not consent if any of those conditions is missing [3]. Best interests is the standard applied to decisions made for a person who lacks capacity, and it is a process, not a single test [1]. Least restrictive is the requirement to prefer the option that interferes least with the person's rights and freedom of action [1]. Coercion covers the means by which compliance is obtained, ranging from persuasion through pressure to legal compulsion. Deprivation of liberty is a legal concept with a specific meaning in England and Wales. An advance decision to refuse treatment and a lasting power of attorney are legal instruments that operate in advance of incapacity, and NICE's depression guideline advises clinicians to consider developing advance decisions and advance statements collaboratively with people who have had recurrent severe depression or depression with psychotic symptoms, recording them and sharing them with the person and, if the person agrees, their family or carer [4].
depth.mechanism: The structural reason these three questions get confused is that in a crisis they arrive at once. Someone is distressed and refusing; there is a risk; there is pressure to act; and the paperwork asks for one box to be ticked. Two mechanisms keep the questions separate. The first is that capacity is bounded to a decision, which means the answer can differ between a decision to accept a blood test and a decision about where to live, taken minutes apart. The second is that consent is constructed rather than captured: the information has to be given in a form the person can use, which is why section 3(2) states that a person is not to be regarded as unable to understand relevant information if they can understand an explanation given in a way appropriate to their circumstances [2]. That provision is not a technicality; it moves the burden onto the person communicating. The third structure is external to the person entirely. Legality of compulsion is supplied by statute rather than by clinical opinion, and the shape of the powers matters. Section 2 of the Mental Health Act 1983 permits admission for assessment where the patient is suffering from mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment, or assessment followed by medical treatment, for at least a limited period, and ought to be detained in the interests of their own health or safety or with a view to the protection of other persons; the application must rest on the written recommendations of two registered medical practitioners, and detention lasts no longer than 28 days [5]. Two things follow that are easy to miss. First, the grounds are about risk and the need for assessment, not about whether the person is refusing; detention is not a remedy for disagreement. Second, the statute's existence does not settle the ethics. The WHO and OHCHR guidance on mental health law proposes a clear mandate for rights-based approaches, argues for deinstitutionalisation and access to community services, and provides concrete measures for eliminating coercion in mental health services in favour of practices that respect rights and dignity [6]. Eliminating coercion is a policy programme precisely because a legal power to coerce does not by itself make coercion desirable, and a service that has the power should still be able to say what less restrictive step was tried, what was not achievable otherwise, and how the restriction will end.
depth.secondExample: Take a fictional inpatient whose family want the care team to manage her money because she is spending it while unwell. The team is asked whether she has capacity, as though there were one question. Break it into several. Can she understand, retain and weigh information about a benefit payment and communicate a decision about it today? If yes, the money decision is hers, even if everyone around her thinks the spending is foolish, and section 1(4) is directly on point. Can she decide about her own accommodation next month? That is a separate question with a different informational load and possibly a different answer. Can she consent to a change in her treatment? A third question, and here her stated views may be given very different weight depending on whether she is detained and what the relevant law allows. The interesting part is not the answer to any one of these questions; it is that a clinician who asks once and writes "lacks capacity" has answered none of them and has created a record that will follow her for years. A second and sharper example is the reverse. A fictional woman is described as "capacity intact, so we can do nothing" after she declines a change in support. That sentence treats capacity as a shield that discharges the service. It is not; a capable refusal of one option leaves the alternatives to be offered, the reasons for refusal to be understood, and the ethical question of what pressure, if any, is legitimate to be answered rather than avoided.
depth.mistake: The four errors that matter most are these. The first is circular reasoning: concluding that someone lacks capacity because they disagree. The second is diagnostic reasoning: treating a mental disorder, a diagnosis, a detention or a presentation as if it established incapacity, when each of those is a separate fact that may be relevant but is not determinative [1]. The third is procedural minimalism: treating consent as a form and information as a document, when the requirement is that the person can use the information, which may require an interpreter, a different format, a supporter, a different time of day, or several conversations [2]. The fourth is what might be called legal abdication, where the presence of a statutory power is treated as the answer to the ethical question. The opposite error matters too, and it is more seductive: reading the principle of respect for autonomy so absolutely that it becomes a refusal to help. Respecting a capable refusal is not the same as abandoning the person, and the obligation to offer alternatives, to revisit the decision when circumstances change, and to be transparent about what the service will and will not do continues throughout.
depth.application: Non-blocking task: take the first fictional case above, the capable refusal, and write it twice. First, write the four-stage capacity reasoning as four sentences, one for each ability, using only what the person has actually said and done. Second, write a coercion audit: list every element of influence in the situation, including how the information was framed, who was present, what was said about the consequences, what the person was told would happen next, and whether any legal power was invoked or implied, and mark each element as agreed, argued, pressured, or compelled, with one sentence of justification. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong capacity analysis cites behaviour rather than conclusions, for example recalling that the person restated the risk estimate in their own words rather than writing "understands". A strong audit contains at least one element the writer initially overlooked, and it names what would be done differently if the person lacked capacity. A weak response writes "patient competent, refused, risks explained" and a weak audit contains the single word "none". If your audit finds no coercion at all in a situation that involved a hospital, a form and a warning about consequences, look again: the point of the exercise is not that coercion is always present, but that it is rarely examined.
depth.summary: Capacity, consent and coercion are three separate problems, and keeping them separate is the discipline the law and the ethics both require. Capacity is a functional, decision-specific and time-specific ability defined by the four abilities in section 3 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, governed by the five principles in section 1, including the assumption of capacity, the requirement to take all practicable steps to help, the irrelevance of unwisdom, best interests, and the least restrictive option [1][2]. Consent is valid only when voluntary, informed and capacitated, and the NHS guidance states that a capable refusal stands even where the outcome may be death [3]. Coercion concerns the means used; statutory powers such as those in section 2 of the Mental Health Act 1983 authorise some of it under narrow, time-limited conditions, and international guidance nonetheless treats the elimination of coercion as a goal, which tells you that lawfulness and justification are different achievements [5][6]. The transferable skill is asking which of the three questions is actually in front of you, and answering that one.

visual.title: Three questions, in order, with the law attached to each
visual.description: A decision diagram that separates capacity, consent and coercion so that each is answered on its own evidence, then recombines them into an action. The diagram marks where statutory powers attach, where best-interests reasoning begins, and where the least restrictive requirement constrains the choice of action.
steps: Step 1, name the decision: write the specific decision in one sentence, including the alternatives and what happens if no decision is made; a vague decision cannot be assessed.

Step 2, capacity for that decision: check the four abilities, understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate, after taking all practicable steps to support the person, and record what the person actually did and said rather than a conclusion.

Step 3, consent: if the person has capacity, ask whether their agreement or refusal is voluntary and informed; if they lack capacity, move to best interests and to the requirement to choose the least restrictive option that achieves the purpose.

Step 4, means audit: list every element of influence actually used, from how information was framed to any legal power invoked, and mark each as agreed, argued, pressured or compelled, with a stated justification for the last two.
Step 5, authority: where compulsion is proposed, name the legal power, its grounds, its duration and its review point, and record what less restrictive step was attempted and what happened.

Step 6, revisit: note the time and circumstances under which capacity will be reassessed, because capacity can change with a delirium, with intoxication, with treatment of a physical cause, or across the day.

lessons.title: Physical illness and mental state: a two-way street with a differential diagnosis attached
lessons.explanation: Psychiatry and general medicine are described as separate specialties, but in the body they are one system, and information flows in both directions. Physical illness can produce mental state changes, including sudden and dramatic ones, and mental state can change the course of physical illness. The clearest single case is delirium, an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over hours to days and fluctuates, and that is caused by an underlying physical condition rather than by a psychiatric disorder. NICE's delirium guideline describes what follows when it is missed: delirium can have serious consequences, including increased risk of dementia and death, and for people in hospital it may increase length of stay and the risk of new admission to long-term care [1]. The guideline treats recognition as everyone's job. People in hospital or long-term care may be at risk, and risk factors to assess at first presentation include being aged 65 or older and having cognitive impairment, with the rule stated bluntly: if any of these risk factors are present, the person is at risk of delirium [1]. Recognition is not a single assessment but a repeated observation, and staff are directed to observe at least daily for recent changes or fluctuations indicating delirium, which may be reported by the person themselves, a carer or a relative, and to document those changes [1]. Where such a change is present, a formal structured assessment follows, and the guideline names particular tools: the 4AT tool, and, in critical care or the recovery room after surgery, the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit or the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist instead [1]. The diagnosis is then made by a healthcare professional with relevant expertise, which may be the same person who made the assessment [1]. Now reverse the direction. NIMH's patient-facing review of chronic disease and depression sets out both arrows. People who have a chronic disease are at higher risk of developing depression, and the listed triggers include anxiety and stress caused by the disease, brain changes from conditions such as Parkinson's disease or stroke, medication used to treat the chronic disease, and a personal or family history of depression or suicide; the review adds that people who have a chronic disease and depression tend to have more severe symptoms of both illnesses [2]. Running the other way, people who have depression are at higher risk of developing certain chronic diseases, including heart disease, diabetes, stroke, pain, osteoporosis and Alzheimer's disease, and NIMH suggests three families of explanation: difficulty completing health-promoting tasks such as eating well and exercising when fatigue is a symptom, difficulty accessing preventive medical care, and changes in the way the body functions, such as increased inflammation, reduced blood circulation and heart rate control, and abnormalities in stress hormones [2]. Those mechanisms are offered as suggestions about why the association exists, not as settled causal chains, and this lesson treats them that way. This is education about clinical reasoning with fictional examples. It does not tell anyone which tests or treatments apply to any real presentation.
lessons.example: A fictional 79-year-old woman is admitted with a hip fracture. On the second night she becomes restless, is not sure where she is, and repeatedly tries to climb out of bed. Two explanations are immediately available. The first is that she is anxious or has developed a psychiatric problem. The second is that she has become acutely confused. The guideline's structural content makes the second explanation the one to work through first, and not because psychiatric explanations are implausible, but because the acute onset, the fluctuation and the context of a hospital admission with a fracture and pain all point towards a physical cause, and because the consequences of missing it are severe [1]. Note also which risk factors are present in the description: age 65 or over, and, if her baseline cognition is impaired, a second risk factor, either of which alone puts her at risk [1]. The clinical reasoning that follows is not a diagnosis, and it does not belong in this lesson. What belongs here is the reasoning discipline: the change is documented, a validated tool is used by someone competent to use it, the diagnosis is made by someone with relevant expertise, and it is recorded both in the hospital record and in the primary care record, an instruction that exists because a delirium that is not communicated becomes a mystery for the next service [1]. Now take a second fictional case in a different direction. A 45-year-old man has three months of fatigue, poor concentration, loss of appetite and low mood. He has been given a diagnosis of depression before, and the temptation is to treat this as a recurrence and to skip the physical review, since the story is familiar. That shortcut is a mistake for a structural reason: fatigue, appetite change, poor concentration and disturbed sleep are features shared by depression and by a wide range of physical conditions, so the symptom set cannot distinguish the explanations on its own. The order of reasoning matters, which is why earlier lessons insisted that medical causes come first, not because they are always the answer but because they are the answer more often than the pattern of symptoms reveals and because missing them is expensive.
lessons.question: An older person in hospital becomes acutely restless and confused at night. Why should the reasoning start with a physical cause rather than with a psychiatric one?
lessons.answer: Because the pattern, acute onset, fluctuation and hospital context, with risk factors such as older age and cognitive impairment, is what delirium looks like, and the consequences of missing it include increased risk of dementia and death.
lessons.distractor: Because distress in hospital is never psychiatric, so a physical cause must be excluded before any mental state change can be taken seriously.
lessons.correction: The guideline does not say that mental state changes in hospital are never psychiatric. It says people in hospital are at risk of delirium, that daily observation for recent changes or fluctuations is required, and that assessment and diagnosis should follow a defined route, with the explicit direction that where delirium, dementia or delirium superimposed on dementia are difficult to distinguish, the delirium is managed first.

depth.definitions: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by an underlying physical condition; the guideline's indicators include recent changes or fluctuations that may be noticed by the person, a carer or a relative, and its named assessment tools are the 4AT, and in critical care the CAM-ICU or ICDSC [1]. A chronic disease, in NIMH's definition, is a condition lasting at least one year that requires ongoing medical attention, or limits activities of daily living, or both, and the examples given include autoimmune diseases, diabetes, cancer, epilepsy, heart disease, HIV/AIDS, hypothyroidism, multiple sclerosis and pain [2]. Diagnostic revision means changing an initial explanation when evidence arrives; it is not a failure but part of the method. Shared features are symptoms such as fatigue, sleep disturbance, appetite change and poor concentration that occur in both psychiatric and physical conditions. Confounding is a factor associated with both a proposed cause and an outcome, producing an association that is not causal. Reverse causation is the possibility that the presumed outcome is in fact the exposure. An explanation is a hypothesis about why this person has this presentation now, and it remains a hypothesis until evidence distinguishes it from its rivals.
depth.mechanism: Three mechanisms explain why the two-way traffic is so hard to read in an individual case. The first is symptom overlap. Fatigue, poor concentration, appetite loss, disturbed sleep and low mood appear in depression and in a long list of physical conditions, so a presentation built from those features is genuinely ambiguous and no amount of careful interviewing resolves it alone. The second is that associations established in populations are weak guides to a single person. NIMH's account of depression raising the risk of conditions such as heart disease, diabetes and stroke is written as a set of possible pathways, and each pathway is a population-level pattern that can be absent, present, or reversed in one individual [2]. The direction of causation may also be genuinely unresolvable from the information available, and it is worth saying plainly that in such cases the answer may not change the plan: if a person has both conditions and both are causing suffering, the work to do may be the same whichever arrow dominates. The third mechanism is that the same ambiguity produces two opposite errors, and both harm people. Treating a physical deterioration as an expression of mental illness leads to delayed care; treating a mental illness as a purely physical matter, or as an inevitable and therefore untreatable consequence of being physically unwell, leads to under-recognition. NICE's depression guideline addresses the second error directly by directing clinicians to be alert to possible depression, particularly in people with a past history of depression or a chronic physical health problem with associated functional impairment, and to consider the two identification questions that ask whether, during the last month, the person has often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless, or by having little interest or pleasure in doing things [3]. The same guideline requires consideration of depression in people with conditions that compromise their ability to communicate, which is where a purely interview-based assessment fails most completely [3].
depth.secondExample: Take a fictional 61-year-old man with a long-standing painful joint condition who is brought in after two weeks of withdrawal from his family, uncharacteristic irritability, and broken sleep. He has a diagnosis of depression from years ago. Four physically-minded explanations and two psychologically-minded ones are all plausible, and it would be a poor lesson that claimed to know which one it was. What can be done is to arrange the information so a wrong guess is cheap. First, separate the features that are unambiguous from the features that are shared. Unambiguous: withdrawal from family, irritability, broken sleep, a change from his baseline. Shared: fatigue, poor concentration, low mood, reduced appetite, and pain, since pain itself disturbs sleep and mood. Second, ask what has changed recently, including any change in the treatment of his physical condition, because NIMH lists medication used to treat a chronic disease among the recognised triggers for depression, which makes a medication review a reasonable question rather than a psychiatric answer [2]. Third, ask which explanation would change the plan if it were true. If the presentation is a recurrence of depression, one set of actions follows; if it is driven by unrelieved pain, a different set follows, and the two are not mutually exclusive. Fourth, set a review point, because both delirium and many physical explanations evolve over days, while depression does not usually appear and disappear within a night. The strategy as a whole is not diagnosis by inference from a list of symptoms; it is arranging for the ambiguity to be resolved by evidence rather than by preference.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first is treating normal investigations as proof of a psychiatric cause; a normal result narrows the differential rather than naming what remains. The second is attributing every physical complaint in a person with a psychiatric diagnosis to that diagnosis, so that a new pain, a new breathlessness or a new confusion is absorbed into the existing story. This is the error the delirium guideline is written to interrupt, and the mechanism of harm is delay [1]. The third is the reverse and is more socially acceptable, which makes it more dangerous: treating depression in the context of physical illness as understandable and therefore not requiring recognition, so that the identification questions are never asked in exactly the group where the guideline says they should be asked first [3]. The fourth is a causal-inference error, in which an association from population research is narrated as a mechanism in one person: because depression is associated with inflammation, this person's depression is described as inflammatory. NIMH offers inflammatory and hormonal pathways as possible explanations for a statistical association, not as findings about individuals, and a formulation that asserts the mechanism has imported certainty the evidence does not contain [2].
depth.application: Non-blocking task: choose one of the fictional cases above and draw a two-column map. In the left column list every feature that is genuinely shared between the physical and the mental explanation, marking each with what it would take to tell them apart, for example a change over time, a corroborating account from someone who knows the person's baseline, or a response to something that is not a psychiatric treatment. In the right column list the features that point one way, with a note of how strong you judge that pointer to be. Then draw two arrows between the columns, one for each direction of influence, and label each arrow with the mechanism as described in the source material being careful to write the word possible or proposed wherever the mechanism is a hypothesis. Finally write one sentence naming the observation that would change your ordering. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong map contains at least one shared feature with no available discriminator, and at least one arrow labelled as a hypothesis rather than a fact. A weak map has only one column filled, or lists a mechanism as established. If your map treats a laboratory or imaging result as decisive, revise: results narrow the differential and do not settle causation.
depth.summary: Physical and mental state influence each other, and the practical consequence is a reasoning rule rather than a slogan. Delirium is the paradigm case of physical illness presenting as a mental state change, and NICE's guideline specifies who is at risk, what to observe and how often, which tools to use, who makes the diagnosis, that it should be documented in both the hospital and the primary care record, and that where delirium and dementia cannot be distinguished the delirium is managed first [1]. In the other direction, NIMH describes a bidirectional association between chronic disease and depression with several possible mechanisms, including disease-related brain changes, medication effects, reduced access to and completion of health care, and physiological changes such as inflammation and altered stress hormone function, all of which should be read as hypotheses about a population-level association [2]. NICE's depression guideline converts this into an action by directing clinicians to be alert to depression particularly in people with a chronic physical health problem and associated functional impairment, and to consider the two identification questions [3]. The transferable principle is that the direction of causation is often undetermined in one person while the duty to keep looking is not.

The two lists are short and are the source for this lesson's bidirectional framing, including brain changes from Parkinson's disease or stroke, medication used to treat a chronic disease, difficulty completing health-promoting tasks, difficulty accessing preventive care, and changes in inflammation, circulation, heart rate control and stress hormones. The section also covers people whose ability to communicate is compromised.
