visual.title: Two arrows, one person: physical illness and mental state as a loop with checkpoints
visual.description: A bidirectional diagram with a physical column and a mental column and labelled arrows in both directions: acute physical disturbance producing delirium, disease-related brain change, treatment effects and functional consequences on one side; reduced health-promoting behaviour, reduced access to preventive care and physiological changes on the other. Each arrow is labelled as established, plausible or hypothesised, and the diagram carries two checkpoints, one for the physical review when a mental state change is acute and fluctuating, and one for the depression identification questions when a physical illness is long-term.
steps: Step 1, describe the change: what is different from this person's baseline, over what period, and who noticed it; acute and fluctuating changes raise a physical cause, while gradual changes raise several possibilities at once.
Step 2, shared features: mark the features that occur in both explanations, such as fatigue, poor concentration, appetite change and sleep disturbance, so they are not counted twice as evidence.

Step 3, physical checkpoint: for an acute mental state change, apply the delirium route, risk factors, at least daily observation of changes or fluctuations, a structured tool used by someone competent, diagnosis by someone with relevant expertise, and documentation in both records.

Step 4, mental checkpoint: for long-term physical illness, ask the two identification questions where depression may be present, particularly with a past history or functional impairment, rather than assuming low mood is explained by the illness.

Step 5, mechanisms: label every proposed pathway with its evidence status, established association, plausible mechanism or hypothesis, and keep medication effects in the list rather than treating them as an afterthought.

Step 6, review: set a short interval when the presentation is acute, because both delirium and many physical explanations change over hours and days, and record what would change your ordering of explanations next time.

lessons.title: Sleep, pain and fatigue: three symptoms that keep exchanging places
lessons.explanation: Sleep, pain and fatigue are the three complaints that most often arrive together, and each of them can be a cause, a consequence, or both. NICE's depression guideline illustrates the difficulty in one line when it lists insomnia and hypersomnia among the perpetuating factors for depression, which is to say that a sleep problem can maintain a mood problem that may also have caused it. The NHS insomnia page supplies the plain definitions and the shape of the problem. Insomnia means regularly having problems sleeping: finding it hard to get to sleep, waking several times, lying awake, waking early and being unable to return to sleep, still feeling tired after waking, finding it hard to nap during the day even when tired, feeling tired and irritable during the day, and finding it difficult to concentrate because of tiredness. Short-term insomnia lasts less than three months and long-term insomnia three months or more. Average sleep need is given as 7 to 9 hours for adults, with the caveat that everyone needs different amounts, and the page's practical marker is that you probably do not get enough sleep if you are constantly tired during the day [1]. The cause lists are where the two-way structure becomes visible. The most common causes of insomnia named by the NHS are stress, anxiety or depression, noise, a room that is too hot or cold, uncomfortable beds, alcohol, caffeine or nicotine, illegal drugs, jet lag and shift work; conditions and medicines that can cause it include mental health conditions such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, Alzheimer's disease or Parkinson's disease, restless legs syndrome, an overactive thyroid, and menopause, alongside many medicines; and among the things that keep people from a good night's sleep the page lists long-term pain, sleepwalking, snoring or interrupted breathing, narcolepsy, and nightmares or night terrors [1]. Long-term pain appears in the insomnia list and disturbed sleep appears in every account of pain, which is the loop in miniature. The same page describes the management direction: insomnia usually improves by changing sleeping habits, and where that does not work a GP may offer cognitive behavioural therapy, in person or through an online self-help programme, to change the thoughts and behaviours that keep a person from sleeping; a referral to a sleep clinic is suggested where there are symptoms of another sleep disorder; and the page notes that GPs now rarely prescribe sleeping pills for insomnia because of serious side effects and dependence, limiting them to a few days or weeks in specific circumstances [1]. This lesson is education about how these symptoms relate. It is not a method for assessing or treating anyone's sleep, pain or fatigue.
lessons.example: Pain gives the second half of the picture, and it comes with a live example of how evidence changes. NICE's low back pain and sciatica guideline recommends advice and information tailored to the person's needs and capabilities to help them self-manage at all steps of the treatment pathway, including information on the nature of low back pain and sciatica and encouragement to continue with normal activities, and it suggests considering a group exercise programme within the NHS for a specific episode or flare-up, taking the person's needs, preferences and capabilities into account [2]. Two recommendations on psychological approaches are no longer there. The published guidance states that NICE removed the recommendation on psychological therapy in July 2026 because a surveillance review found that it might be out of date, but an update was not prioritised in that area, and the same sentence appears against the recommendation on combined physical and psychological programmes [2]. Read that carefully, because it is easy to misread in both directions. The removal is not a finding that psychological therapy does not work for low back pain, and it is not a finding that it does. It means that the committee's earlier statement could no longer be relied upon in its original form and that the area is awaiting re-examination. Anyone who quotes the removal as evidence against psychological treatment for pain, or who continues to quote the old recommendation as current, has misread a procedural decision as a scientific one. Contrast that with the recommendations in the same section that are unambiguous: the guideline states that gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids and benzodiazepines should not be offered for managing sciatica because there is no overall evidence of benefit and there is evidence of harm, and that opioids should not be offered for managing chronic sciatica [2]. Those are statements about evidence of benefit and evidence of harm, and they are the kind of statement that survives being read closely.
lessons.question: NICE removed its recommendation on psychological therapy for low back pain in July 2026. What does that removal establish about whether psychological therapy works for low back pain?
lessons.answer: Nothing either way. The recommendation was removed because a surveillance review found it might be out of date and an update was not prioritised, so the question is currently unexamined rather than answered.
lessons.distractor: It establishes that psychological therapy is ineffective for low back pain, since NICE removes recommendations when the evidence no longer supports them.
lessons.correction: The published wording distinguishes procedure from conclusion: the recommendation may be out of date and the area was not prioritised for update. In the same section, other recommendations are removed for reasons of evidence of harm or absence of benefit, and the contrast in wording is the point.

depth.definitions: Insomnia is a regular difficulty with sleep, defined by NHS content as problems getting to sleep, staying asleep, or waking unrefreshed, subdivided into short-term, under three months, and long-term, three months or more, with average adult need given as 7 to 9 hours and the caveat that individual need varies [1]. Post-exertional malaise is a worsening of symptoms after exertion, and in ME/CFS it is a core symptom; the guideline's terminology distinguishes a flare-up, a transient worsening that typically resolves after a few days, from a relapse, which lasts longer [3]. Energy limit is the amount of energy a person has to do all activities without triggering an increase or worsening of symptoms, and energy management is a self-management strategy of staying within that limit with support from a healthcare professional [3]. Graded exercise therapy is defined in the guideline as establishing a baseline of achievable exercise or physical activity and then making fixed incremental increases in the time spent being physically active, and the guideline notes that it rests on deconditioning and exercise-avoidance theories which assume ME/CFS is perpetuated by reversible physiological changes [3]. Sleep debt is the accumulated difference between sleep obtained and sleep needed. A vicious cycle is a set of mutually reinforcing changes in which each element worsens the next. A perpetuating factor is something that maintains a problem now.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism that makes these three symptoms hard to reason about is mutual reinforcement, and it is worth separating what is well supported from what is plausible. The well-supported part is overlap and co-occurrence. Within a single NHS page, stress, anxiety or depression appear as common causes of insomnia while mental health conditions appear again in the list of conditions that can cause insomnia, and long-term pain appears in the list of things that keep people from sleeping [1]. Direction is therefore not encoded in the co-occurrence itself. The plausible part is the specific loop: pain disturbs sleep, disturbed sleep produces daytime fatigue and low mood, fatigue and low mood reduce activity, reduced activity is followed by deconditioning and further pain. Every link in that chain is individually reasonable, and the chain as a whole is rarely demonstrated in a single person, so a formulation should record which links it is relying on. The second mechanism is that the meaning of fatigue depends on its pattern. In ME/CFS the guideline recognises post-exertional malaise as a core symptom and distinguishes flare-ups from relapses [3], which makes the pattern after activity diagnostically informative in a way that a simple fatigue rating is not. That distinction has consequences: NICE's guideline states that programmes based on fixed incremental increases in physical activity or exercise, including graded exercise therapy, should not be offered as a treatment for ME/CFS, and that cognitive behavioural therapy should be offered only as a supportive intervention and not as a cure, while advising that people should stay within their energy limit rather than pushing through symptoms [4]. The third mechanism is that the same symptom can be a marker of another condition. Sleepiness with snoring or interrupted breathing, sudden falling asleep, and nightmares or night terrors each appear in the NHS page as separate matters rather than as insomnia variants, and the page directs referral to a sleep clinic where symptoms of another sleep disorder are present [1].
depth.secondExample: Two fictional people describe the same two words, tired all the time, and the reasoning that separates them is about pattern rather than intensity. The first is a 29-year-old nurse working rotating shifts who sleeps five or six hours on working days, drinks three coffees before a night shift, and reports that sleep is worst after shifts and better on holiday. Here the fatigue follows the sleep loss and the schedule contains its own explanation, and the useful work is what the NHS page describes: attention to the habits around sleep, with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia offered where habit change alone does not help, and a check for another sleep disorder where the pattern suggests one [1]. The second is a 29-year-old teacher whose symptoms began after an infection, whose sleep is unrefreshing but not short, whose fatigue worsens reliably the day after any exertion, and who describes feeling fluey and wired but tired in the early period [3]. Here the pattern after exertion is the salient fact, and the management direction from the guideline is different in kind: staying within an energy limit rather than building up fixed increments, with cognitive behavioural therapy available as support rather than as a cure [3][4]. Nothing about the two people's fatigue severity tells you which case is which. The differentiating information is the relationship between activity and symptom change, and that relationship is only visible if someone asks about it specifically. Note too what the guideline's own terms imply about caution: it defines graded exercise therapy together with the theories it rests on, and it states that those programmes should not be offered to people with ME/CFS [3][4], which is a rare case of a guideline withdrawing a previously recommended approach because the underlying model did not hold up.
depth.mistake: Five errors are worth naming. The first is assuming a single cause, so that sleep, pain and fatigue are taken to have one explanation rather than several interacting ones. The second is treating a plausible loop as a demonstrated one, and then treating the loop as if it were a cause that can be broken at any point; a formulation should say which link it is acting on and how it will know whether the action worked. The third is universalising the advice: encouraging activity is helpful in many situations and is specifically not the recommended approach for ME/CFS, where fixed incremental increases should not be offered and staying within an energy limit is the framework [3][4]. The fourth is reading a guideline change as a verdict, as in the low back pain case, where a recommendation was removed because it might be out of date rather than because the intervention was shown to fail [2]. The fifth is the assumption that fatigue in the presence of a mental health diagnosis is psychiatric by default, which is the same error discussed in the previous lesson and which is especially costly for people with conditions whose core symptom is post-exertional malaise, given the guideline's own recognition of stigma and of the condition's impact on quality of life [4].
depth.application: Non-blocking task: draw the cycle for one fictional case, with sleep, pain and fatigue as three nodes and arrows in the directions you believe the evidence supports. Label each arrow with one of three markers: supported, plausible, or speculative. Then choose the single arrow you would act on first and justify it in two sentences, including how you would know within a defined period whether the action had helped. Add a fourth node for mood if the case includes it, and mark whether it is upstream, downstream, or both. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong answer has at least one arrow marked speculative and does not exceed one arrow marked supported unless the case documentation actually supports more. A strong justification names a measurable change, for example in the timing of sleep onset relative to the pain, or in the amount of activity the person can do before symptoms worsen, rather than a general improvement. A weak answer draws arrows in one direction only, or proposes a fixed increase in activity for a case whose pattern suggests post-exertional malaise. If your cycle contains no node for circumstances such as shift work, caring responsibilities or housing, add one: the NHS cause list includes noise, room temperature and shift work precisely because these are part of the mechanism rather than background detail [1].
depth.summary: Sleep, pain and fatigue are three symptoms that act on each other, and the honest way to reason about them is to keep the direction and the strength of each link visible. The NHS insomnia material provides the definitions and the cause lists in which mood, sleep, pain, breathing-related problems, medicines and circumstances such as shift work all appear together, and it describes the management direction the health service takes, including cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and a marked reluctance to prescribe sleeping tablets [1]. The low back pain guideline shows the same area being revised in real time, with psychological therapy and combined programmes removed as possibly out of date and other recommendations retained on evidence of benefit and harm [2]. The ME/CFS guideline supplies the concepts that keep fatigue reasoning honest, an energy limit, energy management, post-exertional malaise, flare-up versus relapse, and a defined contrast with programmes of fixed incremental exercise, which should not be offered [3][4]. The transferable rule is that the pattern of a symptom over time is usually more informative than its severity at a single point.

readings.title: NHS, "Insomnia" - sections "Symptoms of insomnia", "What causes insomnia", "Conditions and other things that can cause insomnia" and "Treatment from a GP for insomnia"

visual.title: The sleep, pain and fatigue loop, with every link labelled by evidence strength
visual.description: A four-node cycle linking disturbed sleep, pain, daytime fatigue and reduced activity, with a fifth node for mood, and with each arrow labelled supported, plausible or speculative. Two contrasting patterns sit beside the cycle: a sleep-debt pattern in which the loss of sleep precedes the fatigue and the schedule explains it, and a post-exertional pattern in which symptom worsening follows activity, which changes the management direction.
steps: Step 1, name the nodes: sleep, pain, fatigue, activity and, where present, mood, each with a short description of how it behaves over time rather than a severity rating.
Step 2, label the arrows: for each link write supported, plausible or speculative, and record the observation the label rests on rather than an impression.

Step 3, test the pattern: ask what happens the day after exertion, and ask whether the sleep problem is short, unrefreshing or interrupted by breathing or movements, since these patterns point at different explanations.

Step 4, check the cause lists: medicines, thyroid and menopausal changes, restless legs, mood conditions, shift work, caffeine, alcohol and nicotine all appear among the recognised contributors, and each is a separate question rather than background noise.
Step 5, choose one arrow and one review date: act where the evidence is strongest and the action is reversible, and state what change in the cycle would show that the action worked.

Step 6, respect the exception: where the pattern suggests post-exertional malaise, the direction is staying within an energy limit rather than building fixed increments, and cognitive behavioural therapy is support rather than a cure.

questions.prompt: A trainee writes a discharge summary that lists the timeline, the mental state findings, the social circumstances and the diagnosis, all accurately. A supervisor says the document contains no formulation. What is the supervisor asking for?
questions.answer: An argued account of why these difficulties arose in this person now, with the load-bearing factors identified, their evidence status marked, and a stated implication for the plan.
questions.distractor: A more detailed social history, since a formulation is a summary written in the person's own words rather than the clinician's.
questions.correction: Accurate description is the summary layer. The formulation layer is analytical and evaluative, which is why two clinicians sharing identical notes can produce different formulations, and why a formulation has to state which factor the plan is betting on and how it could be shown to be wrong.

questions.prompt: A fictional patient is judged to need more support. One colleague proposes admission because the person is the most unwell on the caseload; another proposes an intensive home-based crisis service plus a housing worker. Which reasoning decides between them?
questions.answer: Naming the specific unmet needs, checking which setting can meet each one, and identifying the least restrictive option, with a plan containing crisis contact, relapse signs and a review date.
questions.distractor: Choosing the setting with the highest staffing level, because the amount of clinical contact is the best available proxy for unmet need.
questions.correction: Levels of care are different capabilities rather than grades of severity, so the deciding question is what the alternative setting can do that the current one cannot, plus what authority is needed and what the person loses. NICE's transition guideline requires the least restrictive setting that achieves the purpose and specifies what a transition plan must contain.

questions.prompt: A fictional man detained under mental health legislation tells the team he will not accept a proposed change in his accommodation. A colleague writes in the notes that he lacks capacity to decide about accommodation. What is wrong with that entry?
questions.answer: Capacity was concluded from a refusal and from his legal status rather than assessed against the four abilities for that specific decision, and the entry records a conclusion rather than what he said and did.
questions.distractor: Nothing, because a person subject to compulsion cannot exercise capacity while the compulsion continues.
questions.correction: Capacity is functional, decision-specific and time-specific, and detention is a separate fact that may be relevant but is not determinative. The assumption of capacity, the requirement to take all practicable steps to help, and the irrelevance of an unwise decision all apply, and best interests reasoning begins only where capacity to decide that question is absent.

questions.prompt: A fictional 82-year-old with known memory problems becomes agitated and disoriented on the second evening of a hospital admission for a chest infection. A junior clinician suggests a referral to psychiatry for behavioural assessment. What should happen first?
questions.answer: The change should be documented and assessed along the delirium route, since older age and cognitive impairment are recognised risk factors, and the guideline states that where delirium and dementia cannot be distinguished the delirium is managed first.
questions.distractor: An urgent psychiatric referral, because new agitation in a person with cognitive impairment is by definition a behavioural and psychological symptom of dementia.
questions.correction: Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by an underlying physical condition, and the guideline requires structured assessment with a validated tool by someone competent, diagnosis by someone with relevant expertise, and documentation in both the hospital and primary care records. Missing it is associated with increased risk of dementia and death. Psychiatric referral is not excluded; the ordering is what the guideline specifies.

questions.prompt: A fictional patient reports months of spinal pain, unrefreshing sleep and fatigue that is worse for a day after any sustained activity. A colleague proposes a graduated programme of fixed weekly increases in exercise. What is the problem with the proposal?
questions.answer: The pattern of symptom worsening after exertion is the one the ME/CFS guideline identifies as post-exertional malaise, and programmes built on fixed incremental increases in activity should not be offered, with the framework instead being staying within an energy limit.
questions.distractor: There is no problem, because graded increases in activity are the standard approach for chronic pain regardless of the pattern of symptom response.
questions.correction: Activity advice is not universally interchangeable. Pain guidance recommends self-management advice and suggests considering a group exercise programme while taking account of the person's needs and capabilities, and the ME/CFS guideline sets out the energy-limit framework and states that fixed incremental exercise programmes should not be offered for that condition. The pattern after exertion is the information that distinguishes the situations.

units.title: Treatments, other people, and the whole case

lessons.title: Medication classes conceptually: what they target, what they cannot target, and why effects lag
lessons.explanation: Psychiatric medications are taught in classes, and the class names are convenient rather than explanatory. NIMH's public information pages organise the material by class: anti-anxiety medications, including benzodiazepines, beta-blockers used off label for short-term anxiety symptoms and buspirone; stimulants, used for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy; antipsychotics, used for psychosis and, in combination with other medications, for symptoms of delirium and dementia and other conditions more common in older adults; and mood stabilizers, which NIMH notes may also be used to treat depression, usually alongside an antidepressant, as well as schizoaffective disorder, impulse-control disorders and certain conditions in children, with anticonvulsant medications sometimes serving as mood stabilizers because they work better than lithium for some people, such as those with mixed symptoms of mania and depression or rapid cycling [1]. Read that list closely and notice what kind of object a class is. It groups medications by their main proposed target and by the conditions they are used for, and it does not claim that every drug in the class works the same way or works for the same symptoms. This lesson does not tell anyone what to take, when to start, when to stop, or how much of anything to use, and it contains no doses because dosing is not education and belongs with a prescriber who knows the person. What the lesson does is make the timing of effects intelligible, because timing is where most avoidable confusion sits. Three statements can be made from the sources without exaggeration. First, different symptoms within the same condition respond on different timescales. Second, the point at which a treatment should be reviewed is a defined clinical event rather than a matter of patience in general. Third, stopping a medication that has been taken for some time is a process with its own phenomena, which are not evidence that the person is addicted and not evidence that they did not need the medication.
lessons.example: Take the timing evidence. NIMH states that some symptoms, such as agitation and hallucinations, typically go away within days of starting antipsychotic medication, that other symptoms such as delusions usually go away within a few weeks, and that people may not experience the full effects of antipsychotic medication for up to six weeks [1]. The same page notes that buspirone, in contrast to benzodiazepines, must be taken every day for three to four weeks to reach its full effect and is not effective for treating anxiety on an as-needed basis [1]. Now look at the guidance for depression. The NICE depression guideline directs that people starting antidepressant medication should be told about review within about two weeks to check whether symptoms are improving and whether side effects are occurring, with an earlier review a week after starting in specified circumstances, and it requires them to be told why regular monitoring is needed and how often they will need to attend [2]. It states that treatment might need to be taken for at least six months after the remission of symptoms, that it should be reviewed regularly, that some side effects may persist throughout treatment, and that withdrawal symptoms exist and how they can be minimised [2]. On stopping, the same guideline advises people to talk to the prescriber, explains that it is usually necessary to reduce the dose in stages, which it calls tapering, and notes that most people stop antidepressants successfully; it warns that stopping abruptly, missing doses or taking a partial dose can produce withdrawal symptoms, that these do not affect everyone and vary in type and severity, that they can appear within a few days of reducing or stopping and usually go away within one to two weeks, and that they can sometimes be more prolonged [2]. The Royal College of Psychiatrists' patient information says the same things in the register of ordinary language: antidepressants are usually reviewed a few weeks after starting to check how the person feels, whether they are getting side effects, and whether they need to carry on; side effects will usually wear off over a couple of weeks as the body adjusts; early symptoms of agitation, shakiness or anxiety are often why people stop taking an antidepressant, especially if they have not been warned about it; and continuing for at least six months after feeling better reduces the chance of the symptoms returning [3]. It also draws a distinction that patients frequently need: finding it hard to stop is more accurately described as physical dependence, meaning the body has adapted to the medication, than as addiction, which involves craving, loss of control and a high [3].
lessons.question: A person reports no change at all ten days after starting a medication and concludes it does not work for them. What is the most accurate response to the timing question?
lessons.answer: Ten days is too early to conclude anything for the classes and symptoms whose full effects are documented as taking several weeks, so the plan requires a defined review point rather than a verdict now.
lessons.distractor: No response at ten days means the medication is ineffective, since any medication that will work shows measurable benefit within the first week.
lessons.correction: NIMH documents symptom-specific timing, with agitation and hallucinations changing within days, delusions over a few weeks, and full effects for antipsychotics taking up to six weeks, while buspirone requires three to four weeks of daily use. NICE requires an early review of antidepressant treatment at around two weeks. Absence of change at ten days is information to discuss at review, not a settled conclusion.

depth.definitions: A class is a grouping of medications by proposed target, mechanism family or use, and it does not imply that members are interchangeable. Lag or delay of onset is the interval between starting a medication and the appearance of its full effect. Symptom-specific response means that different features of the same condition change at different times. A review point is a scheduled assessment, named in guidance, at which benefit, burden and continuation are reconsidered. Tapering is staged dose reduction over time. Withdrawal symptoms are the effects of reducing or stopping a medication that the body has adapted to, as distinct from addiction, which involves craving, loss of control and a rewarding high, and from relapse, which is the return of the original condition. Monitoring is periodic measurement for a specific known risk, such as weight, glucose and lipid levels for atypical antipsychotics, or lithium levels and kidney and thyroid function for lithium, both of which NIMH notes as regular monitoring requirements [1]. A therapeutic index describes the margin between useful and harmful amounts, and it is the usual reason a medication needs blood monitoring. Harm in a subgroup means an increased rate of an adverse outcome in a defined population, such as the increased rates of stroke and death in older adults with dementia that the United States regulator requires to be stated as a boxed warning on all antipsychotics [1].
depth.mechanism: Why would an effect take weeks? Several explanations are available, and the honest position is that their relative contributions are not settled. The first is symptom specificity: NIMH's account of antipsychotic timing shows that the phenomenon requiring explanation is not one delay but a sequence, with some features resolving in days and others over weeks, which points at the features themselves rather than at a single clock [1]. The second is adaptation, the idea that benefit arises from changes downstream of the immediate target rather than from the immediate effect, which is a model rather than a measurement. The third is measurement and expectancy: early change in a subjective outcome such as mood is influenced by knowing one is being treated, by the natural fluctuation of the condition, and by regression to the mean, so an early improvement is not proof that the medication produced it, and an early absence of improvement is not proof that it will not. The fourth is the accumulation of the medication in the body over days to weeks, a standard pharmacokinetic consideration whose relevance differs between medications and which none of these sources use to explain lag on their own. Two further points belong to the mechanism rather than to the delay. Burden can persist even when benefit arrives: the depression guidance states that some side effects may persist throughout treatment [2], and NIMH names class-level burdens that change the risk-benefit judgement rather than merely annoying the person, including tardive dyskinesia with long-term use of older antipsychotics, the boxed warning about stroke and death in older adults with dementia, dependence and tolerance with long-term benzodiazepine use, and the caution that beta-blockers are generally not recommended for people with asthma or diabetes because they may worsen both conditions [1]. And stopping is itself a phenomenon: the guidance states that withdrawal symptoms can appear within days of reducing or stopping and usually resolve within one to two weeks, with some cases longer [2], while the College's patient information explains the same requirement to reduce slowly and the need in some cases to restart and reduce more gradually [3].
depth.secondExample: Consider three fictional trajectories on the same medication, all of which are commonly misread. In the first, a person feels distinctly better within four days and concludes the medication is working. The honest reading is that the timing is unusually early for the outcome being claimed, and that the improvement may reflect sleep, support, the act of being helped, or the natural course of the episode. That does not make the improvement unreal; it makes the attribution uncertain, and it is worth saying so because a later relapse is often experienced as the medication failing when the early recovery was never attributable to it. In the second trajectory, a person reports no change at three weeks and the medication is stopped and replaced; whether that was right depends on what the review recorded. If the review recorded an adequate trial, an assessment of whether the person actually took it as agreed, and any dose-limiting side effects, then changing treatment is a reasoned decision. If the review recorded only that the person still felt depressed, the trial was not evaluated, it was abandoned. In the third trajectory, a person who had been well stops abruptly, feels dizzy and unsteady with odd electric shock sensations within days, and concludes that the medication was holding them together and that they cannot manage without it. The guidance names exactly this pattern as withdrawal and states that it usually resolves within one to two weeks, which makes the pattern informative about the stopping rather than about the underlying condition [2]. The same guidance notes that most people do stop successfully [2], which is the counterweight to the understandable fear that the third trajectory produces.
depth.mistake: Six errors recur, and the first four are about timing. Treating class membership as mechanism produces predictions that do not hold, because medications grouped together for one purpose differ in their effects and in their monitoring requirements [1]. Treating absence of early response as proof of non-response pre-empts the review that guidance specifies [2]. Treating early improvement as proof of drug effect ignores expectancy, fluctuation and regression to the mean. Stopping abruptly after benefit, on the assumption that the medication is no longer needed, produces the withdrawal pattern that is then misread as relapse [2]. The fifth error is conflating withdrawal with addiction, which the College addresses directly in its explanation of physical dependence as the body having adapted to a medication, contrasted with craving, loss of control and a high [3]. The sixth is the mirror image and is equally harmful: treating withdrawal as nothing, so that a person whose symptoms are prolonged beyond the typical one to two weeks is disbelieved or told they are relapsing. A related error concerns monitoring. Monitoring requirements such as weight, glucose and lipid levels for atypical antipsychotics, or lithium levels with kidney and thyroid function, are not bureaucratic; they exist because the harms being watched for accumulate silently, and a plan that omits them is not a plan [1].
depth.application: Non-blocking task: draw a blank timeline for a fictional person starting a medication, with four vertical markers: the early review, the point at which full effect could reasonably be expected for the target symptom, the point at which continuation decisions are typically reconsidered, and the point at which stopping should be discussed before any change. Under the timeline write four lines, one for each marker, stating what would be recorded at that point: benefit in the target symptom, any side effect and whether it is expected to persist, adherence as the person reports it, and the person's own view of continuation. Then add a fifth line naming the monitoring specific to that medication, if the source material names any. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong timeline distinguishes the timescale for different symptoms rather than applying one date to everything, and its stopping line states that the decision is taken with the prescriber and reduced in stages rather than abruptly. A weak timeline uses a single review date and a single endpoint, or discusses only benefit and not burden. If your timeline leaves the person's own view out, add it: the guidance requires that the person be told about monitoring and about withdrawal, which presumes they are a participant in the decision rather than a recipient of it [2].
depth.summary: Classes are convenient groupings organised around proposed targets and uses, and they carry two kinds of clinical content: what the medication is used for, and what must be monitored because of known harms, such as weight, glucose and lipid levels for atypical antipsychotics, or lithium levels with kidney and thyroid function [1]. Timing is symptom-specific rather than uniform, with agitation and hallucinations changing within days, delusions over weeks and full antipsychotic effects taking up to six weeks, and buspirone requiring three to four weeks of daily use [1]. Guidance supplies the review structure around that uncertainty, an early review at about two weeks for antidepressant treatment with earlier review in specified circumstances, continuation for at least six months after remission, side effects that may persist, and a stoppage process with staged reduction in which withdrawal symptoms can appear within days and usually resolve within one to two weeks [2]. The College's patient information frames the same points in plain language, including the observation that warning people about early agitation is what prevents them from stopping without discussion [3]. The conceptual transfer is that lag converts an immediate judgement into a scheduled review, and that this is a design feature of the evidence and the guidance rather than a defect in the person.

readings.title: NICE NG222, "Depression in adults: treatment and management" - recommendations 1.4.11-1.4.14 on antidepressant medication
readings.note: This is the source for the review timing, the continuation period after remission, the statement that some side effects may persist throughout treatment, and the withdrawal material: talk to the prescriber before stopping, reduction in stages rather than abrupt cessation, symptoms that may appear within days and usually go away within one to two weeks, and the note that most people stop successfully. Read it as a description of what guidance requires clinicians to discuss, not as instruction to any reader, and note that the lesson reproduces the concepts without any dosing. England-specific.

readings.title: Royal College of Psychiatrists, "Antidepressants" patient information - sections on monitoring, side effects, withdrawal and how long to continue
readings.note: Read the section explaining that antidepressants are usually reviewed a few weeks after starting, then the side-effect material, including the observation that early agitation and shakiness are a common reason people stop and that this is why warning matters, and then the sections on how long to continue, on withdrawal and slow reduction, and on the difference between addiction and physical dependence. Written for patients and carers in the UK, which makes it a useful check on whether a technical account is actually intelligible.

visual.title: A medication timeline in four markers, with symptom-specific lag bands
visual.description: A horizontal timeline from the first day of a fictional prescribed medication to a decision about stopping, carrying four markers: early review, expected full effect for the target symptom, continuation review after remission, and stopping discussion. Shaded bands above the line show that different symptoms change at different times, and a lower row lists the monitoring and burden items that must be checked at each marker so that benefit and harm are assessed together.
steps: Day 0 to early review: record what the person was told about timing and about side effects, because guidance requires that they are warned that some early effects are common and usually settle, and that an early review will happen.

Early review: check whether the target symptom is changing, check side effects and whether any are of the kind that may persist rather than settle, and record the person's own account of adherence rather than an assumption about it.

Expected full effect: assess against the timescale documented for that symptom rather than a single date, since some features change within days, others over weeks, and full antipsychotic effects may take up to six weeks, while buspirone needs three to four weeks of daily use.

Continuation review: apply the guidance for the condition, including the requirement that antidepressant treatment might need to be taken for at least six months after remission and reviewed regularly, with monitoring for the specific medication in view.

Stopping discussion: take place with the prescriber before any change, anticipate staged reduction rather than abrupt cessation, and record that withdrawal symptoms can appear within days and usually resolve within one to two weeks, and that physical dependence is not the same as addiction.

Monitoring row: for each marker, name the specific monitoring the source material identifies, such as weight, glucose and lipid levels for atypical antipsychotics, or lithium levels with kidney and thyroid function, so the timeline never shows benefit without burden.

lessons.title: Comparing psychotherapies without crowning a winner
lessons.explanation: The question "which therapy works best" is asked constantly and answered carelessly, in both directions. One careless answer is that all therapies are equivalent, so the choice does not matter. The other is that one modality has won. The guidance itself behaves more carefully than either, and its behaviour is instructive. For a new episode of less severe depression, the NICE depression guideline directs clinicians to discuss treatment options and match the choice to the person's clinical needs and preferences, using its table of options and the accompanying visual summary; it states that all the treatments in that table can be used as first-line treatments, while also directing that the least intrusive and least resource intensive option, guided self-help, is considered first; it requires a shared decision that accounts for the person's preferences; and it recognises that people have a right to decline treatment. In the same section it states that antidepressant medication should not routinely be offered as first-line treatment for less severe depression and should be offered only where that is the person's informed preference [1]. Look at how many distinct claims are packed into that paragraph. There is a set of options treated as equivalent for the purpose of being available first-line. There is an ordering by intrusiveness and resource intensity rather than by efficacy. There is a procedural requirement, shared decision-making. There is a rights claim, the right to decline. And there is a substantive restriction on a medication, qualified by informed preference. This is what a considered position looks like: the table's order reflects the committee's interpretation of clinical and cost effectiveness together with implementation factors, which is stated on the page, and it is not a league table of potency [1]. Where the evidence does speak clearly, the guidance says so, and it is worth seeing both kinds of statement side by side. The PTSD guideline directs that psychologically-focused debriefing should not be offered for the prevention or treatment of PTSD, which is one of the clearest negative recommendations in psychiatric guidance [2]. For the treatment of adults with PTSD or clinically important symptoms presenting more than a month after a traumatic event, the same guideline directs offering an individual trauma-focused cognitive behavioural intervention and names the specific protocols that count: cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy for PTSD, narrative exposure therapy and prolonged exposure therapy [2]. Two of those names describe a technique and two describe a whole protocol, which is itself a lesson in how loose the word "therapy" is. This lesson is education about how to read this evidence. It is not a recommendation about which treatment any person should receive.
lessons.example: The clearest evidence about comparison is not about one therapy beating another; it is about what a trial compares a therapy with. A 2024 meta-analysis by Cuijpers and colleagues pooled 333 randomised controlled trials of psychological treatments for adult depression, comprising 472 comparisons and 41,480 participants, and split them by control condition: 141 trials used a waiting list and 195 used care as usual [3]. The overall effect size at post-test across all comparisons was g = 0.77 with a 95 per cent confidence interval from 0.71 to 0.84 and high heterogeneity, I-squared of 84 [3]. Splitting by control condition produced the finding that matters here: studies with a care-as-usual control group gave g = 0.63, with a confidence interval from 0.55 to 0.71, while studies with a waiting list control gave g = 0.95, with a confidence interval from 0.85 to 1.04, a difference significant at p less than 0.001 that survived every sensitivity analysis including meta-regression adjustment for differences in study characteristics [3]. In proportionate terms, computed from those published figures, 0.95 divided by 0.63 is about 1.51, so the effect size measured against a waiting list is roughly 51 per cent larger than the effect size measured against care as usual, which is a difference in the measurement context rather than in the therapies. The authors' explanation is that the waiting list condition produced less improvement than the care-as-usual condition: within-condition pre-post change was g = 0.37 in the waiting list arms against g = 0.64 in care as usual, while change within the therapy arms was similar across the two sets of trials [3]. Their conclusion is that waiting list control conditions considerably overestimate the effect sizes of psychological treatments and should be avoided in randomised trials of psychological treatment for adult depression [3]. None of this says the therapies do not work. It says that a number quoted without its comparison condition cannot be interpreted, and that reading a batch of effect sizes as though they were measured against the same yardstick is an error of exactly the kind this course has been training you to avoid.
lessons.question: A report describes a psychological therapy as producing an effect size of g = 0.95 for depression. What is missing that would be needed to interpret that number?
lessons.answer: The comparison condition, because the same therapy measured against a waiting list produced g = 0.95 while the pooled estimate against care as usual was g = 0.63.
lessons.distractor: The number of sessions, because all psychological treatments for depression produce equivalent effects once the dose is matched.
lessons.correction: In the 2024 meta-analysis the gap between the waiting-list and care-as-usual estimates was large, significant and robust, and it was explained by less improvement inside the waiting list arms rather than by more improvement inside therapy. The claim that all psychological treatments are equivalent once dose is matched is a stronger position than this evidence supports.

depth.definitions: A modality is a family of therapeutic practice with a shared theory and technique, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, behavioural activation, interpersonal psychotherapy or short-term psychodynamic psychotherapy. A protocol is a specified manualised sequence; trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy as used in the PTSD guideline includes named protocols such as cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy for PTSD, narrative exposure therapy and prolonged exposure therapy [2]. A control condition is the comparator in a trial: a waiting list, where the person receives no treatment for a period; care as usual, where existing care continues; or an active comparator, where the person receives another intervention. An effect size expresses the magnitude of a difference in standardised units, which makes it dependent on both the intervention and the comparator. Heterogeneity describes how much the results differ between studies beyond chance; I-squared is the percentage of variability attributed to that difference, and 84 per cent is high [3]. Allegiance effects describe the relationship between a researcher's preferred model and the results obtained. Common factors are features shared by therapies, such as the alliance, an explanatory framework and a credible rationale, as distinct from the specific techniques of a modality. Shared decision-making is the process of reaching a decision with the person rather than for them [1].
depth.mechanism: Six mechanisms make head-to-head comparison harder than it looks, and they do not all have the same evidential support. The first is the comparator, which is where the strongest evidence sits: the waiting-list and care-as-usual split produced a large and robust difference in the same meta-analysis [3]. The second is what exactly is being compared. Two trials of the same named modality may differ in format, individual or group, in number of sessions, in whether homework is done, and in the experience of the practitioner, and the NICE depression table records features such as who delivers the intervention, how many sessions are involved, and whether homework is needed, precisely because these are part of what is being delivered [1]. The third is outcome selection and the impossibility of blinding: a person cannot be unaware of which therapy they are receiving, and a therapist cannot be unaware of the model they are practising, so expectancy and allegiance cannot be eliminated, only described. The fourth is the common factors debate, in which one position holds that specific techniques carry the effect and another holds that shared features do most of the work; this is genuinely contested, and the safest formulation is that both classes of factor are present and their relative contributions are unresolved. The fifth is who enters trials: eligibility criteria select particular presentations, so a result applies to a population similar to the one studied, which is why guidance often attaches conditions such as a presentation more than one month after a traumatic event [2]. The sixth is the shape of the recommendation, which is not binary. Guidance offers, considers, restricts and prohibits, and it conditions some options on prior non-response, as with EMDR for children and young people aged 7 to 17, which the PTSD guideline offers only if they do not respond to or engage with trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy [2]. A prohibition, such as the one on psychologically-focused debriefing [2], means the evidence does not support the practice; it is not automatically a statement that the practice is toxic.
depth.secondExample: Consider two fictional people asking the same question, which therapy is best for me, and see how differently a careful answer is shaped. The first is a 34-year-old with PTSD symptoms that began after an assault eight months ago, who avoids the area where it happened and has intrusive images. The guidance's answer is unusually specific: an individual trauma-focused cognitive behavioural intervention is offered, and the named protocols that fall under it are listed [2]. The second is a 34-year-old with a new episode of depression of less severe severity, whose difficulties include low mood, withdrawal and loss of pleasure but no traumatic event. Here the guidance's answer is a set of options that may all be used first-line, ordered by intrusiveness and resource intensity, reached by shared decision with the person, with a right to decline, and with medication restricted to the situation where it is the person's informed preference [1]. The two situations are not equivalent, yet both are described in ordinary conversation as needing therapy. The differences in the answers come from four things: what condition is being treated, what evidence exists for that condition, what the guidance's committee judged about implementation and cost, and how specific the effective protocols are. A fifth factor sits outside the evidence but inside the decision: what the person can practically attend, and what they are willing to do. The PTSD guideline acknowledges the last of these directly, noting that people with PTSD may be apprehensive, anxious or ashamed, may avoid treatment, may believe it is untreatable, or may have difficulty developing trust, and it names engagement strategies such as following up missed appointments and allowing flexibility in attendance policies [2]. A modality that the person cannot attend is not the best modality for that person, which is a statement about delivery rather than about efficacy, and it belongs in the comparison.
depth.mistake: Five errors recur. The first is the dodo-bird overreach: because several modalities show benefit, concluding that all are interchangeable and the choice is arbitrary. The guidance does not say that; it restricts, conditions and prohibits in some circumstances and lists protocols by name in others [1][2]. The second is the opposite, promoting one modality as the only evidence-based option, which is not compatible with a table whose entries are all usable first-line [1]. The third is reading an effect size without its comparator, which the waiting-list and care-as-usual gap shows to be a real and quantified error [3]. The fourth is treating the absence of a recommendation as evidence of harm; the removal of a recommendation because it may be out of date and the prohibition of debriefing are different statements, and neither is a finding of harm. The fifth is forgetting that trial populations are selected, so that a strong result in a studied group is generalised to people who would not have been eligible, including people with substance use, cognitive impairment, unstable housing, or more than one condition at once. A sixth, related error belongs to the reader of this lesson: assuming that a psychological treatment is free of adverse effects because it is psychological. Trials capture dropout, deterioration and distress during exposure-based work, and a formulation that treats therapy as costless will fail to look for them.
depth.application: Non-blocking task: take three fictional presentations from earlier in this course and for each write three lines. Line one: the modality families named by guidance for that presentation, if any. Line two: the condition the guidance attaches, such as a time since the event, a severity threshold, or a prior non-response. Line three: one thing that cannot be concluded from the evidence you have. Then add a fourth line to exactly one of the three: the comparison condition you would want in a trial designed to answer the remaining question, and why that comparator rather than another. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong answer names at least one guidance condition, contains at least one line stating a limit rather than a conclusion, and justifies the comparator by reference to what the comparison changes about the measured effect. A weak answer names a single best therapy, or writes that all therapies are equally effective, or omits the condition attached to a recommendation. If none of your three lines mentions the person's preference or capacity to attend, add one, because the guidance builds both into the decision and treats the right to decline as explicit [1].
depth.summary: Guidance does not crown a single winner. It offers a set of options that may all be used first-line for less severe depression, orders them by intrusiveness and resource intensity, requires a shared decision, recognises the right to decline, and restricts medication to situations of informed preference [1]. Where the evidence is specific it becomes specific, naming trauma-focused protocols for adults with PTSD and offering EMDR to children and young people only after trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy has not been engaged with, while prohibiting psychologically-focused debriefing [2]. And comparison itself has been shown to be comparator-dependent: in a meta-analysis of 333 trials and 472 comparisons, the pooled post-test effect against care as usual was g = 0.63 while against a waiting list it was g = 0.95, a difference of roughly 51 per cent, explained by less improvement in the waiting list arms rather than more in therapy [3]. The transferable rule is to ask three questions of any claim that one therapy is better than another: better for whom, measured against what, and on which outcome.

visual.title: A comparison grid for therapy claims: modality, population, comparator and outcome
visual.description: A four-column grid in which each row is one claim that a therapy works, with columns for the population studied, the comparison condition used, the outcome measured, and the direction and size of the recommendation in guidance, whether offered, considered, restricted to a later line, or prohibited. A second panel shows the same therapy's estimate shifting from g = 0.95 against a waiting list to g = 0.63 against care as usual, making the comparator column visibly load-bearing.
steps: Step 1, population: write who was studied, including the eligibility conditions such as time since a traumatic event or a severity threshold, because the result belongs to that group.

Step 2, comparator: write what the therapy was compared with, waiting list, care as usual, or another active treatment, and note that the same therapy produced different estimates depending on this column.
Step 3, outcome: write which outcome was measured and by whom, and note that blinding of participants and therapists is not possible in psychological treatment trials.

Step 4, recommendation shape: label the guidance statement as offered, considered, restricted by prior non-response, or prohibited, since these are different strengths and only the last is an absence of support for the practice.

Step 5, alternative explanations: list the candidates that could account for the result, including expectancy, allegiance, therapist effects, dose and format, and mark which are contested rather than settled.
Step 6, decision line: write what the person can and will attend, because access and preference enter the decision alongside the evidence, and the right to decline is explicit in guidance.

lessons.title: Families and carers: partnership, burden and the real limits of confidentiality
lessons.explanation: Families and carers are treated in guidance as partners and are also subject to the most misunderstood rule in mental health care. Start with who they are, because the stereotypes are wrong. The Royal College of Psychiatrists' information for carers states that carers can be of any background, that they may themselves experience physical or mental health problems, that they do not always live with the person they care for, and that they may support them often, occasionally or by telephone; it also distinguishes carers, meaning unpaid family, partners or friends, from care workers who are employed to provide support. Carers may look after a parent or parent-in-law, a partner or spouse, their children whether adult or under 18, another relative such as a grandparent, a friend or a neighbour, and some care for more than one person with different levels of need [1]. The kinds of support they provide are wider than the word caring suggests: practical help with cooking, cleaning, laundry and shopping; healthcare-related help with taking medication, attending appointments and physiotherapy; emotional support and company; social support such as transport; financial help with money, care services and benefits; personal help with washing, bathing and using the toilet; and physical help with moving around the home [1]. Now the confidentiality rule, which is where most distress and most error occurs. The College's page explains that everyone has a right to confidentiality about their health information, that this means individuals decide who accesses their information, and that healthcare professionals are legally required to keep it private [1]. It then lists the circumstances in which information might be shared even without the person's agreement: if the patient says they can; if it would be in the best interests of a patient who lacks the capacity to make that decision; if it is required by law; or if it will protect the patient or other people from harm. Even in those circumstances, the page states that professionals should share only the information that is necessary, share only with the people the patient has consented for, and record how and why the information was shared [1]. The asymmetry that follows is the part people most often miss: a carer can almost always give information to professionals, even when professionals cannot give information back. The College states that carers can pass on information they think would be helpful, that this is allowed even where professionals cannot share information with them, and that unless the person has asked professionals not to talk or listen to them, they should listen and consider how it might help with care and treatment [1]. This lesson is education about these structures and the reasoning behind them, using fictional examples. It is not legal advice, it is not guidance for any particular situation, and it does not tell anyone what to disclose.
lessons.example: Take a fictional case and run it twice. A carer telephones a community team because their partner, who has been under the team for a year, missed an appointment and has been sleeping through the day. The carer asks what the team is doing about the missed appointment and what the plan is. In the first version, the person has not agreed to any information being shared, and nothing in the source material permits disclosure on the facts described. The workable response has several parts and none of them is "I cannot speak to you". The professional can receive the information the carer offers, since the College's page says carers may share information and that professionals should listen unless the person has asked them not to. They can explain that they cannot confirm or discuss the person's care without agreement, in plain language, and say why. They can ask whether the carer has any view about what the person would allow to be shared, and they can plan to check consent with the person at the next contact, revisiting it rather than treating it as fixed. They can offer the carer general information about what the service does, and carer support, since the Triangle of Care standards include a carer introduction to the service, a range of carer support services, and a defined post responsible for carers [3]. And they can record what was said. In the second version, the person has agreed that the team may tell their partner about appointments and about the plan, but not about anything discussed in private sessions. Now the same phone call allows confirmation that an appointment was missed, discussion of how the team will follow up, and nothing about the content of sessions. The distinction is not bureaucratic fussiness. It is the difference between a general permission and a specific one, and it is the mechanism by which a person keeps control of what is known about them while still allowing the people around them to help. The framework published by the General Medical Council gives the same structure at the level of professional standards. It begins from the statement that confidentiality is an important ethical and legal duty but is not absolute, and sets out the circumstances in which personal information may be disclosed without breaching confidentiality, which are: the patient consents, whether implicitly or explicitly, for their own care or for local clinical audit, or explicitly for other purposes; the disclosure is of overall benefit to a patient who lacks capacity to consent and is made in line with the relevant capacity legislation; the disclosure is required by law, or is permitted or approved under a statutory process that sets aside the common law duty; or the disclosure can be justified in the public interest [2]. It distinguishes explicit consent, where a patient actively agrees orally or in writing, from implied consent, where it would be reasonable to infer agreement, and it states that in other cases explicit consent should be sought unless it is not appropriate or practicable, giving examples such as a risk of serious harm to the person seeking consent, circumstances where seeking consent would undermine the purpose of the disclosure, or situations where action must be taken quickly [2]. It adds that if information is disclosed without consent, there must be a legal basis for breaching confidentiality [2].
lessons.question: A carer asks for details of their partner's care and has no agreement from the partner that information may be shared. What can the professional lawfully do?
lessons.answer: Receive and consider the information the carer provides, decline to confirm clinical details, explain why, seek the person's consent for future sharing, offer carer support and general information, and record what was done.
lessons.distractor: Explain that confidentiality is absolute, so nothing can be shared in any direction and the carer should raise their concerns directly with the person instead.
lessons.correction: The duty is not absolute and the flow of information is asymmetric rather than blocked. Carers may give information even when professionals cannot give it back, unless the person has asked professionals not to talk or listen to them, and disclosure without consent is permitted only on the bases set out in the framework, which were not met on these facts.

depth.definitions: A carer, in the sense used by the Royal College and by NICE, is an unpaid family member, partner, friend or neighbour providing support; this is distinct from care workers who are employed to provide care [3]. Confidentiality is the duty to keep personal health information private, held by the person the information is about. Explicit consent is active agreement, orally or in writing, while implied consent is a reasonable inference of agreement from the circumstances [2]. Overall benefit is the standard used for disclosure about a patient who lacks capacity, applied in line with capacity legislation [2]. Public interest justification is a separate basis on which disclosure may be justified when the benefit to an individual or to society outweighs the public and the patient's interest in confidentiality [2]. The minimum necessary principle is the requirement to disclose only what is necessary and only to those the person has agreed [1]. Carer burden describes the physical, emotional, financial and social costs of providing care. The Triangle of Care is a quality improvement scheme run by Carers Trust for health and social care providers that promotes safety, recovery and wellbeing by including and supporting unpaid carers, organised around six standards [3]. Service-user involvement is the practice of the person using services participating in decisions about their own care [4].
depth.mechanism: Why is the rule shaped this way? Three structures explain it. The first is that the right being protected belongs to the person receiving care. Confidentiality exists so that people can seek help without losing control of who knows what, and that protection is not weakened because a relative is well intentioned. The second is that information about the person and information about the carer are different objects. A carer asking about their own situation, support options, or how to manage a particular behaviour is asking about something that does not require the patient's consent to answer, whereas a carer asking what the team has decided is asking about the patient. Much of the perceived unfairness dissolves at that distinction, though not all of it, and the residue is real: the carer is doing the work and holds less of the information. The third structure is that consent is revisitable, granular and often assumed to be all or nothing. The framework's categories, implicit consent for direct care, explicit consent for other purposes, and the conditions on which disclosure without consent is permitted, all presuppose that someone has actually determined what the person agrees to rather than settling the question once [2]. Guidance builds participation directly into care processes so that the question is answered routinely rather than at the moment of crisis. NICE's transition guideline requires that a designated person be responsible for writing the care plan in collaboration with the person being discharged and with their carers if the person agrees, that group psychoeducation support for carers be considered during discharge planning with signposting to information about the person's specific condition, that changes in carers' circumstances since admission be taken into account, and that before discharge carers are told about the plan, have the person's progress and readiness discussed with them, and know the likely date well in advance [4]. The Triangle of Care scheme takes the same logic upstream by requiring that carers are identified at first contact or as soon as possible afterwards, that staff are carer-aware and trained in carer engagement, that policy and practice protocols for confidentiality and information sharing exist, that defined posts are responsible for carers, that a carer introduction to the service is available, and that a range of carer support services exists [3]. Protocols and named posts matter because the alternative is that each interaction is improvised by whoever answers the phone.
depth.secondExample: Take the same fictional situation from the other side and see what changes. The carer in this version is the only person who sees the person every day, and reports that for two weeks the person has been eating very little, has stopped opening the curtains and has twice mentioned that there is no point going on. The professional has no agreement to share anything back. Under the framework, receiving that information is straightforward and its content is clinically important, because a carer's account of change over time is often the only longitudinal information available. What the professional does next is not a disclosure question but an assessment question: whether the reported change meets any threshold that requires action, which in the first instance means assessing the person. The disclosure rule does not stand in the way, because assessing the person does not require telling the carer anything. Now change the scenario slightly. The carer reports that the person has described a specific plan, using legal terminology, and that there are means available in the house. The framework's categories include a disclosure justified in the public interest, and the narrow question of whether that basis is met is a professional judgement supported by the framework's own examples, where seeking consent may be inappropriate because it would put someone at risk of serious harm or would undermine the purpose of the disclosure [2]. The important structural point is that the framework anticipates this and gives conditions rather than a prohibition [2][1]. The mirror-image error also deserves stating: treating a carer's account as noise because they are emotionally involved. The College's page reflects the opposite expectation, that professionals should listen and consider how the information might help, and the Triangle of Care's rationale is that carers can provide vital insight into the treatment and condition of those they care for [1][3].
depth.mistake: Five errors recur. The first is describing confidentiality as absolute, which is both inaccurate and unhelpful, because the framework states that the duty is not absolute and lists the bases on which disclosure may be made [2]. The second is the opposite failure, disclosing to a helpful relative as an act of kindness without a basis, and without recording the reason; the College's material requires that even permissible sharing be limited to what is necessary, to those agreed, and recorded with the reasons [1]. The third is failing to distinguish the two directions of travel, so that a carer who is entitled to be heard is treated as if they were making an improper request, or a professional's inability to answer is experienced as a refusal to care. The fourth is settling consent once and treating it as permanent, including treating a person's initial refusal as final; consent is granular and revisitable, and a professional who never re-asks has decided for the person that the answer will not change. The fifth is burden blindness. The College's own description of carers includes people with their own health problems supporting more than one person across several kinds of care, and the Triangle of Care page reports an estimated seven million unpaid carers in the United Kingdom, of whom it states 13 per cent support people with mental health conditions, which would be roughly 910,000 people on those figures alone [1][3]. A service that treats carers purely as sources of information and never as people with needs of their own will also get worse information, because the relationship it is relying on will not survive.
depth.application: Non-blocking task: write two things. First, a four-sentence script for a fictional telephone call in which a carer asks for information the professional cannot give, containing: an acknowledgement of the carer's information and its value, a plain statement of what cannot be shared and why, one thing the professional can do, and a specific commitment to revisit consent. Second, a two-column list of what could be shared without the person's consent in that situation, which in most circumstances will be general service information and carer support rather than anything about the individual, and what could be shared if the person agreed, marked with the level of agreement needed. Model response and self-review rubric: a strong script contains the words that make the restriction understandable rather than impersonal, includes receiving information as an action rather than as a courtesy, and names a person or process the carer can contact. A weak script either over-explains the law to a distressed caller or gives details without a basis. If neither column mentions recording the decision, add it: the College's material and the professional framework both require that sharing, and the reasons for it, be recorded [1][2].
depth.summary: Families and carers are partners with their own needs, and the confidentiality rule that governs what they can be told is narrower than they often expect and less absolute than they are often told. The person receiving care holds the right, so access to information depends on consent, on capacity and overall benefit, on legal requirement, or on a public interest justification, and even then only what is necessary is shared, only with those agreed, and the reasons are recorded [1][2]. The asymmetry is real and legal: carers may give information even when they cannot receive it, and professionals are expected to listen and consider what it might contribute [1]. Guidance builds partnership into process rather than leaving it to goodwill, with named responsibility for the care plan, carer psychoeducation and signposting, attention to changes in carers' circumstances, and specific expectations about what carers are told before discharge [4], while the Triangle of Care scheme converts the same principles into six standards and a named post [3]. The transferable skill is being able to say what cannot be shared, and why, without treating the person asking as an obstacle.

visual.title: Two directions of travel: what a carer may give and what a professional may return
visual.description: A two-lane diagram between a carer on one side and a service on the other. The carer-to-service lane is open and labelled with the requirement that professionals listen and consider the information unless the person has asked them not to.
